tool_args.old_string: Large Language Model (LLM) evaluation results vary across reproductions, but variance sources interact, and their relative importance shifts with the benchmark format. No study has simultaneously crossed infrastructure and methodology facets in a unified factorial design across benchmarks. We apply Generalizability theory (G-theory) in a crossed design with up to seven facets across eight open-weight 7--9B parameter instruction-tuned models and five benchmarks, totaling approximately 2.3 million cross-model evaluation records. A recommended 3-prompt $\times$ 3-seed design achieves $G \geq 0.80$ with 178 items (1,602 total evaluations per model), a 3.1$\times$ item reduction over single-condition designs (552 items, 552 evaluations). Under binary scoring, BF16 and FP16 numerical precisions are functionally interchangeable ($<$0.1\% interaction). Model$\times$item interaction (up to 36\%) is the second-largest component in cross-model analysis, indicating that models differ primarily in which items they find difficult. Preliminary scale validation across a 24$\times$ parameter range (3B--72B) confirms stable variance structure within one architecture family. We observe suggestive but statistically underpowered format-associated differences in variance concentration that warrant investigation with larger benchmark samples. We release an open-source G-theory pipeline and D-study budget calculator for evaluation design optimization.
tool_args.new_string: Large Language Model (LLM) evaluation results vary across reproductions, but variance sources interact, and their relative importance shifts with the benchmark format. We apply Generalizability theory (G-theory) in a fully crossed design with up to seven facets across eight open-weight instruction-tuned models (7--9B parameters) and five benchmarks, totaling approximately 2.3 million evaluation records. D-study projections show that a recommended multi-condition design achieves $G \geq 0.80$ with 178 items (1,602 evaluations per model), a 3.1$\times$ item reduction over single-condition designs (552 items, 552 evaluations)---trading approximately 3$\times$ more evaluations per item for 3$\times$ fewer items, a tradeoff that favors multi-condition designs when item construction is costly. Model$\times$item interaction (up to 36\%) indicates that models differ primarily in which items they find difficult, not in overall ability. We observe suggestive but statistically underpowered format-associated differences in variance concentration between multiple-choice and free-form benchmarks. We release an open-source G-theory pipeline and D-study budget calculator for evaluation design optimization.

1	Large Language Model (LLM) evaluation results vary across reproductions, but variance sources interact, and their relative importance shifts with the benchmark format. We apply Generalizability theory (G-theory) in a fully crossed design with up to seven facets across eight open-weight instruction-tuned models (7--9B parameters) and five benchmarks, totaling approximately 2.3 million evaluation records. Format constrains the noise floor, but difficulty heterogeneity determines variance magnitude within it.
